Under HIPAA Safe Harbor (45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)), all 18 identifiers must be removed—including exact calendar dates (keeping only year), ages >89 (aggregated into a single 90+ category), and 3-digit zip codes whose geographic unit contains <=20,000 people (replaced with 000). Under federal AKS, lived-experience advisors may be compensated at documented Fair Market Value ($100-$250/hr in low-burden 30-45 min sessions) strictly decoupled from any prescribing or clinical-trial referral volume.

question: A digital-pathology startup has trained a WSI AI algorithm that quantifies continuous bone-marrow reticulin fiber density and megakaryocyte spatial topology in Myelofibrosis (overcoming ~30-40% manual WHO grading discordance). Distinguishing FDA's Drug Development Tool (DDT) / RDEA biomarker qualification process from CDRH medical-device clearance, which regulatory and commercialization sequence is accurate?

choices.A: Completing FDA DDT biomarker qualification automatically confers CDRH 510(k)/De Novo clinical diagnostic marketing clearance, enabling immediate commercial hospital pathology billing without any RUO clinical-trial phase or separate CDRH device submission.
choices.B: FDA DDT qualification follows two stages (Pre-IND meeting -> NDA approval) and qualifies the algorithm universally across all fibrotic solid and hematologic organs simultaneously without a defined Context of Use (COU).
choices.C: Monetize first as RUO trial biomarker SaaS ($300K-$1.5M/trial) while building longitudinal data for FDA's 3-stage DDT pathway (Letter of Intent -> Qualification Plan -> Full Qualification Package for a COU) and parallel 510(k)/De Novo SaMD.
choices.D: Complete CLIA Laboratory Developed Test (LDT) analytical validation first, because CLIA LDT validation legally substitutes for FDA DDT/RDEA surrogate biomarker qualification across Phase 3 registrational myelofibrosis trials.
choices.E: Apply to FDA's Rare Disease Endpoint Advancement (RDEA) pilot solely after securing De Novo SaMD clearance, because RDEA is restricted strictly to post-commercial diagnostic devices and bars pre-pivotal sponsor engagement.
choices.F: Launch immediately as Non-Device CDS under 21st Century Cures Sec. 3060 to bill Medicare Part B hospital pathology codes while submitting unconsented commercial WSI scans to satisfy FDA's Full Qualification Package.

explanation: FDA Drug Development Tool (DDT) biomarker qualification (21st Century Cures Sec. 3011) follows a formal 3-stage pathway—Letter of Intent (LOI), Qualification Plan (QP), and Full Qualification Package (FQP)—to qualify a biomarker for a tightly defined Context of Use (COU) in drug development, which is legally distinct from CDRH 510(k)/De Novo SaMD clinical marketing clearance. Commercially, monetizing first as RUO centralized trial biomarker SaaS ($300K-$1.5M/trial) generates immediate B2B biopharma revenue while accumulating prospective multi-center outcome correlations needed for both DDT/RDEA surrogate qualification and eventual CDRH SaMD clearance.

question: A myeloid-inflammation biotech plans to expand its lead oral JAK/IRAK1/mTOR-axis asset sequentially across three ultra-rare/rare hematologic diseases sharing academic centers and marrow biology: Primary Myelofibrosis (ORPHA:824), VEXAS syndrome (UBA1, ORPHA:597743, NCT05027945), and siltuximab-refractory iMCD (ORPHA:93685, NCT03933904)—without seeking any non-orphan indication. Integrating 21 CFR 316 and the July 4, 2025 ORPHAN Cures Act (Pub. L. 119-21) amendment to IRA Medicare price negotiation, what is the exact exclusivity and pricing-protection outcome?

choices.A: Under 21 CFR 316, all three rare indications share a single 7-year exclusivity clock starting at the first PMF approval, and adding VEXAS immediately forfeits IRA Medicare negotiation exemption under the 2025 ORPHAN Cures Act.
choices.B: Each rare indication earns an independent 7-year US orphan exclusivity clock from its own approval date, but under current post-July-2025 federal IRA statute, securing a second orphan approval STILL immediately forfeits Medicare negotiation exemption.
choices.C: Stacking PMF, VEXAS, and iMCD earns independent 7-year ODD clocks AND grants permanent IRA Medicare negotiation exemption even if the sponsor later obtains FDA approval for broad rheumatoid arthritis (>1M US patients).
choices.D: Each rare indication earns an independent 7-year US ODD clock from its approval date while reusing CMC/Phase 1 data, AND under the July 4, 2025 ORPHAN Cures Act (Pub. L. 119-21) it retains IRA Medicare exemption while exclusively orphan.
choices.E: FDA bars holding more than two active Orphan Drug Designations for the same active moiety under 21 CFR 316.25, forcing the sponsor to synthesize a distinct deuterated analog before submitting the third (iMCD) orphan filing.
choices.F: Under the July 4, 2025 ORPHAN Cures Act, multi-indication orphan drugs retain IRA Medicare exemption strictly if approved as biologics (BLA), whereas small-molecule oral therapies lose exemption upon their second orphan indication.

explanation: Under 21 CFR 316, a single molecule can stack separate, independent 7-year US orphan market exclusivity clocks for each distinct rare disease (PMF, VEXAS, iMCD), running from each indication's approval date while reusing CMC, GLP tox, Phase 1 PK, and academic hematology infrastructure. Critically, whereas the original 2022 IRA stripped Medicare Drug Price Negotiation exemption upon a second orphan approval, the ORPHAN Cures Act—signed July 4, 2025 (Pub. L. 119-21)—amended the IRA so drugs and biologics designated and approved exclusively for ONE OR MORE rare diseases retain exemption (losing it only if approved for a non-orphan indication).

question: On September 3, 2025, FDA CDER and CBER jointly launched the Rare Disease Evidence Principles (RDEP) framework. Which exact combination of population cutoff, biological eligibility criteria, evidentiary standard, and procedural timing accurately defines RDEP?

choices.A: Applies to any orphan disease (<200,000 US patients), lowers the statutory 'substantial evidence of effectiveness' bar to preclinical + case reports, and is requested at NDA/BLA submission without post-marketing requirements.
choices.B: Targets <1,000 US patients with a known genetic defect causing rapid disability/death and no adequate therapy; meets 'substantial evidence' via 1 study + confirmatory evidence + PMRs, requested before pivotal launch.
choices.C: Applies exclusively to CBER viral gene therapies affecting <5,000 US patients (excluding CDER small molecules and ASOs), requires two single-arm trials plus external controls, and waives all post-marketing commitments.
choices.D: Targets populations <1,000 US patients across both acquired autoimmune and monogenic diseases, permits approval without any adequate and well-controlled human study when animal PD is definitive, and is filed at End-of-Phase-2.
choices.E: Targets populations <1,000 US patients with a known genetic defect, mandates a randomized sham-control arm unless natural history exceeds N=500, and applies only after an Accelerated Approval confirmatory trial stalls under FDORA.
choices.F: Applies to populations <10,000 US patients with progressive genetic or sporadic neurodegeneration, replaces FDA's 2023 Confirmatory Evidence guidance with automatic Breakthrough + RMAT designation, and is requested at NDA filing.

explanation: Jointly introduced by CDER and CBER on September 3, 2025, the Rare Disease Evidence Principles (RDEP) apply to ultra-rare populations (generally <1,000 US patients) caused by a known in-born genetic defect driving progressive, rapid disability or death with no adequate disease-altering therapy. RDEP does NOT lower the statutory 'substantial evidence of effectiveness' bar; instead, it clarifies that one adequate and well-controlled study (often single-arm) paired with robust confirmatory evidence (pathophysiologic correction, clinical PD/biomarkers, relevant models, natural history/external controls) plus PMRs can satisfy it—with sponsors expected to apply BEFORE launching the pivotal trial.

disease_family: Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC) & Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD)
harm_mechanism: Launching an Accelerated Approval orphan drug without a feasible confirmatory trial underway risks post-commercial recruitment collapse (as in Ocaliva/COBALT) and expedited withdrawal under FDORA.
question: In December 2022, Congress enacted FDORA Section 3210 to overhaul Accelerated Approval following delayed or failed confirmatory studies such as eteplirsen's MIS51ON (NCT03992430) and obeticholic acid's (Ocaliva) COBALT trial in PBC (NCT02308111, ORPHA:186). Which exact combination of FDORA Section 3210 statutory powers and Ocaliva/COBALT forensics is accurate?

choices.A: FDORA Sec. 3210 requires confirmatory trials to finish enrollment before Accelerated Approval, mandates annual (365-day) progress reports, and bans ALP surrogates; Ocaliva won full PBC approval after COBALT succeeded in non-cirrhotics.
choices.B: FDORA Sec. 3210 lets FDA require confirmatory trials underway at approval with quarterly (90-day) enrollment progress reporting, yet preserved legacy multi-year formal administrative hearings prior to market withdrawal; Ocaliva withdrew solely over payer pricing.
choices.C: FDORA Sec. 3210 requires confirmatory studies underway within 3 years post-approval plus 180-day progress reporting, while COBALT failed strictly because obeticholic acid failed to lower serum alkaline phosphatase in Phase 3 POISE.
choices.D: FDORA Sec. 3210 prohibited FDA from granting Accelerated Approval to non-oncology orphan diseases, forcing PBC and DMD sponsors onto traditional outcomes endpoints after Ocaliva's COBALT trial revealed excess cardiac mortality.
choices.E: FDORA Sec. 3210 authorized 180-day progress reporting and expedited withdrawal, yet explicitly exempted Orphan Drug-designated products from the 'confirmatory trial underway' gate; Ocaliva remained marketed for non-cirrhotic PBC.
choices.F: FDORA Sec. 3210 lets FDA require confirmatory trials underway at approval, mandates 180-day progress reports, and streamlines expedited withdrawal—illustrated by Ocaliva's stalled COBALT study, non-cirrhotic liver-injury/death signal, CRL, and withdrawal.

explanation: FDORA Section 3210 (Dec 2022) granted FDA four interlocking Accelerated Approval enforcement levers: (1) explicit authority to require confirmatory trials to be underway before approval (or within a set period); (2) authority to specify enrollment targets, protocols, and completion milestones; (3) mandatory progress reports every 180 days starting <=180 days post-approval; and (4) streamlined expedited withdrawal procedures. Ocaliva (PBC, ORPHA:186) exemplifies the peril: after 2016 ALP-based Accelerated Approval, its placebo-controlled COBALT trial (NCT02308111) struggled to recruit post-commercial launch and stopped early, safety analyses showed excess liver injury/transplant/death even in non-cirrhotic patients, FDA issued a CRL denying full approval, and Ocaliva was withdrawn from the US market.

disease_family: Hemophilia A/B & Systemic AAV Gene Therapies
harm_mechanism: Underwriting systemic AAV gene therapy without modeling pre-existing capsid NAb exclusion, GMP COGS, durability decay, and prophylactic incumbents drives commercial collapse and abandoned patient access.
question: Multiple approved gene therapies suffered commercial retreat or market withdrawal—including Glybera, Zynteglo (EU exit), Roctavian (Hemophilia A, NCT03370913), and Pfizer's 2025 discontinuation of Beqvez (Hemophilia B, NCT03861273, ORPHA:98879) within a year of FDA approval. Which mechanistic, CMC, and commercial synthesis accurately identifies the vectors and root causes of this collapse?

choices.A: Beqvez (AAV Hemophilia A) and Roctavian (AAV Hemophilia B) failed because pre-existing anti-AAV neutralizing antibodies exclude >85% of adults and neither achieved measurable clotting factor expression in pivotal Phase 3 trials.
choices.B: Zynteglo (systemic AAV beta-thalassemia), Roctavian, and Beqvez collapsed commercially primarily because FDA's 2024 biosimilar guidance removed 12-year BPCIA exclusivity for viral-vector biologics, triggering biosimilar price erosion.
choices.C: Beqvez (Hemophilia B) and Roctavian (Hemophilia A) failed solely because anti-AAV NAbs exclude <5% of adults while requiring myeloablative busulfan conditioning, driving patients back toward weekly intravenous FVIII/FIX.
choices.D: High GMP COGS and $2.8M-$3.5M single-payment shock hit 30-50% anti-AAV NAb exclusion, transaminitis/FVIII durability decay (Roctavian), EU HTA deadlock (ex vivo lentiviral Zynteglo), and convenient prophylactic incumbents (emicizumab, EHL, marstacimab).
choices.E: Roctavian (Hemophilia A) and Beqvez (Hemophilia B) both showed permanent >100% factor durability with zero transaminitis, failing commercially solely because CMS barred state Medicaid programs from reimbursing hemophilia gene therapies.
choices.F: Commercial retreat stemmed strictly from GMP batch contamination at BioMarin and Pfizer rather than payer budget shock or incumbent prophylaxis, as emicizumab is FDA-approved solely for Hemophilia B patients with factor inhibitors.

explanation: Approval does not ensure commercial survival in gene therapy: Roctavian (AAV5 Hemophilia A, NCT03370913), Beqvez (AAV-Spark100 Hemophilia B, NCT03861273; discontinued in 2025 with zero commercial patients dosed), and Zynteglo (ex vivo lentiviral beta-thalassemia—NOT AAV—pulled from EU over HTA pricing deadlock) collided with high GMP COGS, $2.8M-$3.5M one-time payer shock, 30-50% pre-existing anti-capsid NAb exclusion, steroid-requiring transaminitis/DRG toxicity and waning FVIII durability, and safe, convenient chronic prophylactic incumbents (emicizumab, extended-half-life factors, marstacimab).

disease_family: Rare Pediatric Diseases vs. Adult-Onset Orphan Diseases
question: In 2026, a venture fund diligences two novel-active-ingredient (NME) orphan assets: Asset X for pediatric Dyskeratosis Congenita / Telomere Biology Disorders (ORPHA:1775) and Asset Y for adult Primary Myelofibrosis (ORPHA:824). Applying FDCA Section 529 (Rare Pediatric Disease PRV), operational redemption requirements, and the 2024-2026 legislative reauthorization timeline, which diligence model is exact?

choices.A: Only Asset X (NME; serious <200K disease primarily ages 0-18) earns a freely transferable PRV (10->6 mo review; >=90-day notice + user fee), reauthorized Feb 3, 2026 through Sept 30, 2029 after Dec 20, 2024 lapse; adult Asset Y is ineligible.
choices.B: Only Asset X qualifies for a PRV (cutting review 10 -> 6 mos with 30-day advance notice and zero additional FDA redemption fee), transferable exactly once before the program's reauthorized statutory sunset on September 30, 2027.
choices.C: Both Asset X and Asset Y qualify once granted FDA Orphan Drug Designation and a pediatric study plan, with unlimited transferability (~$100M-$160M resale) and a permanent non-sunsetting statutory authorization enacted on February 3, 2026.
choices.D: Only Asset X qualifies—including if developed as a 505(b)(2) repurposed active moiety—provided the sponsor notifies FDA >=180 days prior to redemption and submits the BLA before the December 20, 2026 statutory sunset deadline.
choices.E: Only Asset X qualifies (cutting FDA priority review from 12 months down to 3 months with >=90-day advance notice), subject to a statutory cap barring third-party voucher resale above $100M under the February 3, 2026 Consolidated Appropriations reauthorization.
choices.F: Neither Asset X nor Asset Y can earn a PRV in 2026 because the Rare Pediatric Disease PRV statute permanently expired on December 20, 2024 without Congressional reauthorization, leaving only Tropical Disease and MCM vouchers active.

explanation: Under FDCA Sec. 529, a Rare Pediatric Disease PRV requires: (1) a novel active ingredient (no previously approved active moiety—excluding repurposed 505(b)(2) moieties), (2) a serious/life-threatening rare disease (<200,000 US) whose serious manifestations primarily affect ages 0-18 (Asset X qualifies; adult PMF Asset Y does not). Vouchers have unlimited transferability ($100M-$160M market value), compress FDA review by 4 months (10 -> 6 mos), and require >=90 days' advance notice plus an annual PRV redemption user fee on top of PDUFA fees. After lapsing on Dec 20, 2024, Congress reauthorized the program on Feb 3, 2026 (Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 / Mikaela Naylon Give Kids a Chance Act) through Sept 30, 2029.

disease_family: SMA, X-ALD, MPS I & Infantile Krabbe Disease
harm_mechanism: Assuming federal RUSP addition immediately delivers nationwide newborn screening causes commercial launch miscalculation and leaves infants in lagging states to miss the presymptomatic curative window.
question: Following FDA approvals of presymptomatic therapies for X-ALD (ORPHA:43, RUSP 2016), SMA (ORPHA:83330, RUSP 2018), and Infantile Krabbe disease (ORPHA:487, RUSP 2024), why does US real-world newborn identification still exhibit a multi-year 'zip-code survival gap', and what exact multi-tier assay architecture is required to implement Krabbe screening without overwhelming families with false positives?

choices.A: Federal RUSP addition legally binds all 50 states within 180 days, so delays reflect solely parental opt-outs; Infantile Krabbe screening relies exclusively on first-tier GALC enzyme activity without second-tier metabolite biomarkers.
choices.B: RUSP is non-binding and typically requires 12-18 months for full 50-state screening rollout; Infantile Krabbe uses first-tier dried-blood-spot qPCR SMN1 deletion testing followed by second-tier C26:0-LPC tandem mass spectrometry confirmation.
choices.C: RUSP is federally binding once CMS issues a Medicaid DRG code (usually 2 years); Krabbe requires first-tier psychosine MS/MS followed by second-tier whole-genome sequencing to filter benign GALC pseudodeficiency alleles.
choices.D: Because HHS RUSP mandates uniform federal lab equipment purchases, states lag primarily over IRB consent rules; Krabbe screening pairs first-tier GALC enzyme activity with second-tier serum galactosylceramide ELISA assays.
choices.E: HHS RUSP is non-binding: states independently legislate, fund, and validate multi-tier assays (e.g., first-tier GALC enzyme + second-tier psychosine MS/MS in Krabbe to filter pseudodeficiencies/late-onset cases), causing 5-to-6+ yr lags.
choices.F: RUSP is non-binding, driving a 5-to-6+ year state-by-state lag, yet SMA (added 2024) and Infantile Krabbe (added 2018) both rely strictly on single-tier dried-blood-spot qPCR without second-tier metabolite confirmation.

explanation: Addition to the federal HHS Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP)—X-ALD in 2016, SMA in 2018, Infantile Krabbe disease in July 2024—is strictly advisory, not a federal mandate. All 50 states must separately legislate, fund appropriations, purchase MS/MS or qPCR platforms, build specialist follow-up networks, and validate multi-tier assays—such as first-tier GALC enzyme activity paired with second-tier psychosine MS/MS in Infantile Krabbe to prevent overwhelming families with benign GALC pseudodeficiency alleles and late-onset variants. Consequently, full 50-state adoption historically takes 5-6+ years.

disease_family: CLN7 Batten Disease & Nano-Rare Genetic Disorders
question: Following the N-of-1 development of milasen for a single child with a unique MFSD8 intronic splicing variant in CLN7 Batten disease (ORPHA:228366; PMID:31597037), FDA issued dedicated 2021 guidance for individualized antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs). Which exact nonclinical/regulatory streamlining did FDA permit, and why do these economics still break traditional venture-backed biotech models?

choices.A: FDA waived all animal toxicology entirely for N-of-1 splice-switching ASOs under sponsor-investigator INDs, yet traditional VCs still avoid the category because FDA caps bespoke reimbursement at $500,000 per treated patient.
choices.B: FDA mandated full two-species 6-month GLP toxicology plus a 12-month controlled efficacy extension before dosing any N-of-1 ASO, pushing costs above $15M and blocking both venture firms and nonprofits like n-Lorem.
choices.C: FDA allowed streamlined sponsor-investigator INDs (single-species 3-month GLP tox + class-knowledge CMC), yet $1M-$2M+ bespoke tox/GMP costs cannot amortize across 1-30 patients with no NDA or PRV payout, requiring nonprofits like n-Lorem.
choices.D: FDA allowed single-species 3-month GLP tox under a commercial NDA track awarding a transferable Rare Pediatric Disease PRV per unique mutation, yet VCs pass because PRV resale requires >=500 treated commercial patients.
choices.E: FDA streamlined milasen (targeting CLN2 TPP1) via a 28-day single-species non-GLP screen, yet traditional VCs pass because individualized ASOs are statutorily barred from Medicare Part B buy-and-bill reimbursement.
choices.F: FDA restricted its 2021 individualized ASO guidance exclusively to IV hepatic GalNAc-siRNA therapeutics using single-species 3-month GLP toxicology, explicitly excluding intrathecal CNS splice-switching ASOs like milasen from streamlined CMC.

explanation: Milasen (Kim et al., NEJM 2019, PMID:31597037; MFSD8 splicing mutation in CLN7 Batten disease, ORPHA:228366) catalyzed FDA's 2021 individualized ASO guidance, which allows sponsor-investigator INDs for severely debilitating/life-threatening nano-rare diseases to leverage well-characterized chemistry-class safety (e.g., 2'-MOE phosphorothioate) for a streamlined single pharmacologically relevant species 3-month GLP toxicology study and fit-for-purpose CMC. Even streamlined, custom sequence screening, GLP tox, and GMP synthesis cost ~$1M-$2M+ per unique mutation with N=1-30 global patients and no commercial NDA or RPD PRV payout—breaking VC economics and requiring charitable models like n-Lorem.

question: A biotech attempts two Orphan Drug Act maneuvers: (1) seeking ODD for a broad anti-inflammatory small molecule by restricting enrollment to a 12% biomarker slice (<200,000 patients) of a 1.2M-patient disease where outside patients could still respond; and (2) launching a reformulated version of an already-approved orphan drug after its 7-year exclusivity expires to claim a fresh 7-year exclusivity block. Under 21 CFR Part 316, what exact legal tests govern both requests?

choices.A: 21 CFR 316.20(b)(6) rejects salami-slicing unless drug properties make outside patients inappropriate ('orphan subset'), and 21 CFR 316.3(b)(3) requires clinical superiority for a 'same drug' to break OR earn 7-yr exclusivity.
choices.B: 21 CFR 316.20(b)(6) approves any biomarker subset <200,000 once paired with a PMA companion diagnostic, while 21 CFR 316.3(b)(3) requires proving clinical superiority ONLY to break active exclusivity—not to earn new 7-yr exclusivity post-expiry.
choices.C: 21 CFR 316.20(b)(6) bars all biomarker-defined subsets of non-rare diseases unconditionally even with mutation-specific binding, while 21 CFR 316.3(b)(3) accepts a >=30% WAC price reduction as a 'major contribution to patient care'.
choices.D: 21 CFR 316.20(b)(6) requires proving outside patients would suffer fatal toxicity (efficacy differences cannot justify an orphan subset), while 'same drug' under 21 CFR 316.3(b)(14) applies strictly to identical salts and never biologics.
choices.E: 21 CFR 316.20(b)(6) rejects artificial salami-slicing unless the sponsor runs a head-to-head trial in the broader 1.2M population, while 21 CFR 316.3(b)(3) grants automatic 7-year exclusivity to any once-daily reformulation of a twice-daily tablet.
choices.F: Under 21 CFR Part 316, FDA accepts arbitrary prevalence slicing whenever clinical protocols exclude other subtypes, and awards a fresh 7-year exclusivity block whenever a subsequent sponsor shows statistical non-inferiority to the expired pioneer.

explanation: Two strict 21 CFR Part 316 rules block Orphan Drug Act gaming: (1) Under 21 CFR 316.20(b)(6), a sponsor cannot artificially 'salami-slice' a >=200,000 disease into a <200,000 subset unless inherent properties of the drug (mechanism, toxicity profile, or mutation-specific binding) make patients outside the subset inappropriate candidates ('orphan subset'); and (2) under 21 CFR 316.3(b)(3) and FDA Reauthorization Act (FDARA) codification, a subsequent 'same drug' (same active moiety/principal molecular structural features) must prove clinical superiority—greater effectiveness, greater safety in a substantial portion of the target population, or major contribution to patient care (never mere lower price)—both to break active exclusivity AND to earn its own fresh 7-year exclusivity even after the pioneer's exclusivity expires.

question: A repurposing startup obtains a method-of-use patent for an off-patent generic 10 mg oral tablet in a severe orphan autoimmune disease and cites GSK v. Teva (Fed. Cir. 2021) to tell Series A investors that Hatch-Waxman Section viii skinny labels are effectively dead, protecting a $150,000/yr price. What exact legal holding of GSK v. Teva and Hatch-Waxman vs BPCIA exclusivity matrix refutes this pitch?

choices.A: GSK v. Teva abolished Section viii carve-outs nationwide, so the startup's method-of-use patent DOES protect $150,000/yr pricing once paired with 5-year NCE exclusivity on an unmodified 10 mg 505(b)(2) new-indication filing.
choices.B: GSK v. Teva held that skinny-label generics incur automatic induced-infringement liability whenever clinicians write off-label scripts, yet 3-year clinical exclusivity expires too quickly to justify $150,000/yr orphan pricing.
choices.C: Section viii (505(j)(2)(A)(viii)) carve-outs apply exclusively to 12-year BPCIA biosimilars and not to small-molecule generic ANDAs, so generic 10 mg tablets remain legally barred from retail pharmacy substitution until the method-of-use patent expires.
choices.D: Although GSK v. Teva upheld induced infringement solely on active promotional statements, a 505(b)(2) NDA for the exact 10 mg tablet receives 5-year NCE exclusivity that blocks all existing generic pharmacy substitutions.
choices.E: GSK v. Teva upheld induced infringement (35 U.S.C. 271(b)) ONLY on Teva's active marketing—leaving silent Section viii skinny labels intact; an unmodified tablet gets <=3-yr (not 5-yr NCE/12-yr BPCIA), needing differentiated 505(b)(2) + 7-yr ODD.
choices.F: Because the U.S. Supreme Court reversed GSK v. Teva on certiorari in 2023, generic manufacturers now enjoy absolute statutory immunity to actively market patented orphan indications alongside Section viii skinny labels.

explanation: In GlaxoSmithKline v. Teva (Fed. Cir. 2021; Supreme Court denied cert), the Federal Circuit upheld $235M+ in induced-infringement damages (35 U.S.C. 271(b)) specifically on totality-of-the-circumstances evidence that Teva's press releases, catalogs, and marketing actively promoted the carved-out patented indication—NOT by abolishing Section viii (505(j)(2)(A)(viii)) skinny labels when generics stay silent and pharmacies substitute cheap legacy strengths. Furthermore, an unmodified generic moiety gets at most 3-year clinical investigation exclusivity (neither 5-year NCE nor 12-year BPCIA biologic exclusivity), so VC-grade commercial repurposing requires a differentiated 505(b)(2) strength/formulation/prodrug + 7-year ODD exclusivity (or nonprofit Every Cure/CDCN execution).

harm_mechanism: Enrolling a biomarker-selected Phase 3 trial via local LDTs without banking both positive and negative screened specimens invalidates CDx concordance bridging and risks a CRL.
question: A rare-disease biotech enrolls its pivotal biomarker-selected Phase 3 trial using local academic CLIA Lab-Developed Tests (LDTs) rather than a locked commercial Companion Diagnostic (CDx), and prospectively banks residual tissue ONLY from biomarker-positive enrolled patients (discarding biomarker-negative screen failures) while delaying IVD PMA co-development. What exact regulatory and biostatistical failure occurs at NDA/BLA filing?

choices.A: Banking 100% of biomarker-positive enrolled specimens fully satisfies CDRH PMA bridging requirements for both PPA and NPA, so the sole regulatory risk is a 30-day administrative delay to open a Diagnostic Master File (MAF).
choices.B: FDA automatically grandfathers CLIA LDTs used in pivotal rare-disease trials into nationwide Class III PMA companion diagnostics, requiring concordance bridging only when migrating from PCR to whole-genome sequencing.
choices.C: FDA expects contemporaneous Class III PMA CDx approval (via MAF); discarding biomarker-negative screen-failure specimens prevents unbiased NPA and discordant-call efficacy bridging, risking a CRL absent a serious-disease post-marketing exception.
choices.D: CDRH requires prospectively banking ONLY biomarker-negative specimens (not positive enrolled patients) to prove analytical specificity, and federal law bars therapeutic sponsors and IVD partners from sharing assay data via a Diagnostic Master File (MAF).
choices.E: Companion diagnostics selecting rare somatic driver mutations are universally classified as Class I exempt devices rather than Class III PMAs, so local LDT enrollment creates zero CRL risk even without banked archival specimens.
choices.F: Because FDA statutorily forbids approving any drug prior to contemporaneous CDx PMA approval without exception—even in fatal ultra-rare diseases—discarding negative specimens permanently invalidates the Phase 3 therapeutic efficacy readout.

explanation: Under FDA's IVD Companion Diagnostic Co-Development Guidance, CDER/CBER and CDRH expect contemporaneous approval of a validated commercial CDx (typically Class III PMA, coordinated confidentially via a Diagnostic Master File, MAF) whenever the test is essential for safe/effective patient selection. Crucially, an LDT/CTA-to-CDx bridging study must re-test BOTH biomarker-positive enrolled patients AND a representative cohort of biomarker-negative screen failures so positive/negative percent agreement (PPA/NPA) and clinical efficacy under discordant LDT-/CDx+ sensitivity analyses remain unbiased; omitting banked negative specimens risks a CRL or label delay (unless FDA grants its narrow serious/life-threatening post-marketing CDx commitment exception).

disease_family: Regenerative Cell & Gene Therapies (US vs. EU Strategy)
question: A gene-therapy SME planning parallel US FDA and EU EMA regulatory filings compares FDA's Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy (RMAT, 21st Century Cures Sec. 3033) designation against EMA's PRIority MEdicines (PRIME) scheme. Which exact matrix of modality scope, entry evidence gate, review timeline, and exclusivity accurately distinguishes RMAT from PRIME?

choices.A: FDA RMAT spans all small-molecule and biologic modalities using preliminary clinical data, whereas EMA PRIME is restricted exclusively to Advanced Therapy Medicinal Products (ATMPs) and cuts MAA active review from 210 to 90 days.
choices.B: FDA RMAT permits SMEs to qualify on compelling non-clinical animal POC data alone and grants 10-year US exclusivity, whereas EMA PRIME strictly requires Phase 2 randomized clinical efficacy data from every applicant.
choices.C: Both FDA RMAT and EMA PRIME automatically confer Accelerated Approval / Conditional Marketing Authorization upon designation, waive GMP potency comparability, and compress agency review clocks to 120 active days.
choices.D: FDA RMAT requires preliminary clinical evidence and explicitly bars post-approval real-world evidence or registry confirmation, whereas EMA PRIME assigns an early CHMP/CAT rapporteur and grants 12-year EU orphan exclusivity.
choices.E: EMA PRIME applies across all modalities with early SME non-clinical entry and cuts active review from 180 to 120 days, whereas FDA RMAT applies to cell/gene therapies only after Phase 3 enrollment is 100% complete.
choices.F: FDA RMAT covers cell/tissue/gene therapies with preliminary clinical data (adding surrogate/RWE confirmation); EMA PRIME spans all modalities, accepts SME non-clinical POC, assigns an early rapporteur, and unlocks 150 vs 210-day review (no exclusivity).

explanation: Under 21st Century Cures Sec. 3033, FDA RMAT applies strictly to regenerative medicine therapies (cell therapies, tissue-engineered products, human gene therapies) with preliminary CLINICAL evidence for serious/life-threatening conditions, conferring Breakthrough Therapy benefits plus explicit statutory Accelerated Approval via surrogate/intermediate endpoints and post-approval RWE/registry confirmation. EMA PRIME spans ALL therapeutic modalities, permits SMEs and academic sponsors to enter earlier on compelling non-clinical + tolerability/early POC data, appoints an early CHMP/CAT rapporteur for iterative Scientific Advice, and unlocks Accelerated Assessment (150 vs 210 active review days). Neither designation itself grants market exclusivity.

question: A single-dose Sickle Cell Disease (ORPHA:232) gene therapy launches at a $2,200,000 AMP/WAC. Calculate its baseline federal Medicaid Drug Rebate Program (MDRP) statutory minimum rebate floor, explain why a legacy 100% single-patient outcomes refund broke commercial contracting, and specify how 42 CFR 447.505 Multiple Best Price and the 2025 CMS CGT Access Model resolved this impasse.

choices.A: Baseline Medicaid rebate is 13.0% of AMP ($286,000); legacy single Best Price capped manufacturer refunds at 50%, whereas 42 CFR 447.505 waives all Medicaid rebates for CGTs across the 12 states in the 2025 CGT Access Model.
choices.B: Baseline innovator rebate is 23.1% of AMP ($508,200); one legacy 100% refund reset national Best Price to ~$0, whereas 42 CFR 447.505 allows outcome-tiered prices (offered to all states) and the 2025 CGT Access Model (33 states+DC+PR; ~84% Medicaid SCD) pools OBAs.
choices.C: Baseline innovator Medicaid rebate floor is 17.1% of AMP ($376,200) across all gene therapies; 42 CFR 447.505 Multiple Best Price applies automatically even if offered to one commercial payer, while CMS CGT Access is mandatory in all 50 states.
choices.D: Baseline innovator Medicaid rebate floor is 23.1% of AMP ($508,200), but CMS's 2025 CGT Access Model (15 participating states) replaced outcomes-based rebates with 10-year federal patient co-insurance loans while repealing 42 CFR 447.505 reporting.
choices.E: Baseline innovator Medicaid rebate floor is 23.1% of AMP ($440,000); legacy single Best Price applied strictly to Medicare Part D plans, whereas 42 CFR 447.505 Multiple Best Price caps maximum manufacturer outcomes rebates at 23.1% across all 33 participating states.
choices.F: Baseline innovator Medicaid rebate floor is 30.0% of AMP ($660,000); Multiple Best Price under 42 CFR 447.505 excludes single-dose cell and gene therapies, forcing CMS to negotiate cash-only upfront discounts without clinical outcome tracking.

explanation: Under the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program, the statutory baseline rebate floor for single-source innovator drugs is 23.1% of AMP (note: 13% is generics; 17.1% applies strictly to clotting factors and exclusively pediatric drugs)—equaling $2,200,000 x 0.231 = $508,200 per dose. Under legacy single Best Price, offering a 100% outcomes refund for one failed patient reset national Medicaid Best Price to ~$0 across every Medicaid patient. Revised 42 CFR 447.505 allows manufacturers offering a VBP arrangement to all states to report multiple outcome-tiered Best Price points without contaminating baseline pricing, and CMS's voluntary 2025 CGT Access Model (33 states + DC + PR, covering ~84% of US Medicaid SCD beneficiaries) centrally negotiates multi-state outcomes-based rebates plus standardized access criteria and ancillary support (e.g., fertility preservation and travel).

question: To cross the rare-disease preclinical-to-Phase 1b 'valley of death' without crippling early dilution, orphan founders combine federal translational programs (NCATS BrIDGs/TRND, FDA OOPD R01 grants, NIH SBIR/STTR, CIRM) with patient-foundation venture philanthropy (modeled on the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation [CFF]-Vertex partnership, ORPHA:586). Which exact operational mechanic distinguishes each funding engine?

choices.A: NCATS BrIDGs/TRND award unrestricted $3M cash grants to founders in exchange for 20% federal royalties, FDA OOPD R01s fund exclusively preclinical mouse toxicology, and CFF acquired 51% common voting equity in Vertex before selling shares for $3.3B.
choices.B: NCATS BrIDGs/TRND supply in-kind GMP/GLP IND-enabling services while taking exclusive federal patent ownership, CIRM awards impose zero California spending requirements, and CFF invested $15M to realize $330M in Vertex royalties in 2014.
choices.C: FDA OOPD clinical-trial grants fund exclusively post-approval Phase 4 registries, NCATS BrIDGs operates solely for viral gene therapies, and CFF structured its $150M Vertex support as non-repayable academic fellowships with zero royalty return.
choices.D: NCATS BrIDGs/TRND supply in-kind GMP/GLP IND support (non-cash, no equity/IP); FDA OOPD R01s fund clinical trials (Phases 1-3); SBIR/STTR & CIRM grant non-dilutive funds; CFF invested ~$150M in Vertex for royalties sold for $3.3B in 2014.
choices.E: NCATS BrIDGs/TRND provide in-kind GLP/GMP services for cash-matching 50% equity warrants, NIH SBIR/STTR covers Phase 3 clinical trials without caps, and CFF monetized its $150M Vertex investment via a $3.3B Rare Pediatric Disease PRV auction in 2014.
choices.F: FDA OOPD R01 grants fund preclinical target discovery while NCATS BrIDGs funds Phase 3 pivotal clinical trials in-kind, and CFF's $150M Vertex contract was barred by IRS 501(c)(3) rules from recycling royalty proceeds into future CF research.

explanation: Understanding exact translational mechanics prevents wasted applications: NCATS BrIDGs and TRND do NOT give cash grants or take equity/IP—they deploy NIH-contracted in-kind GMP manufacturing, formulation, and GLP toxicology to fill IND-enabling gaps; FDA OOPD Orphan Products Grants (R01) specifically fund clinical trials (Phases 1-3, not preclinical mouse work); NIH SBIR/STTR and CIRM (California-nexus regenerative medicine) provide non-dilutive grants; and CFF's venture-philanthropy archetype invested ~$150M directly into Aurora/Vertex in exchange for structured product royalties—monetized for $3.3B in 2014 to recycle into next-generation CF cures.
